name: Black Consciousness Movement
info: The Black Consciousness Movement was a grassroots anti-apartheid movement that emerged in South Africa in the mid-1960s, led by Steve Biko, and sought the psychological liberation of black people through pride, black leadership and community programmes.

facts.where: South Africa, especially its universities, townships and churches, with strong activity in Durban and Soweto; community programmes in the Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal
facts.period: emerged in the mid-1960s; University Christian Movement 1966; Black Community Programmes 1970; strikes and protests 1972–1973; bans and arrests from 1973; Soweto uprising 1976; Biko's death and the banning of its organisations 1977; AZAPO founded 1978; ideas and successor groups continuing today
facts.figures: Steve Biko, its founder and primary leader; Barney Pityana; Mamphela Ramphele; Bennie Khoapa; Mapetla Mohapi, director of the Zimele Trust Fund; Aubrey Mokoape and Patrick Lekota, among the SASO nine; the poets Mongane Serote and Mafika Gwala
facts.outcome: it did not bring down apartheid and its organisations were banned in 1977, but its ideas spread through most of black South African politics and the Azanian People's Organisation (AZAPO) persists

t: The movement held that black liberation would come not only from political and structural change but from a psychological transformation in which black people believed in the value of their blackness.
It asked white allies to understand and support, but not to lead, and it defined black to include South Africans of Indian descent and other people of colour.

Many of its leaders were banned or imprisoned and its organisations were outlawed in 1977, a month after Steve Biko died in police custody, yet its language and strategy spread through most corners of black South African politics.
dyk: By 19 June 1976, three days after the Soweto uprising began, 123 key members of the movement had been banned and assigned to internal exile in remote rural districts.
ev: An Anglican meeting convened under Archbishop Robert Selby Taylor leads to the University Christian Movement, which becomes the vehicle for Black Consciousness
Steve Biko, Barney Pityana, Mapetla Mohapi, Mamphela Ramphele and Bennie Khoapa establish the Black Community Programmes as self-help groups
The government begins to clamp down, and virtually the entire leadership of SASO and the Black Community Programmes is banned
Leaders are arrested under the Terrorism Act after rallies in support of the FRELIMO government in Mozambique
Black children march in Soweto against Afrikaans-medium teaching and security forces kill 176 protesters by the official count
Steve Biko dies in police custody on 12 September
On 19 October, known as Black Wednesday, 19 groups associated with the movement are declared illegal
The Azanian People's Organisation is formed and its chairman and secretary are soon detained under the Terrorism Act

sections.background:
The Black Consciousness Movement emerged in South Africa in the mid-1960s out of the political vacuum created by the jailing and banning of the African National Congress (ANC) and Pan Africanist Congress leadership after the Sharpeville massacre of 21 March 1960. The brutality of Sharpeville caused many black people to embrace the idea of violent resistance, and the ANC's armed wing, Umkhonto we Sizwe, began its campaign in 1962, but no victory was in sight by the time Steve Biko was a medical student in the late 1960s. The ANC had been banned, and although the Freedom Charter stayed in circulation, for many students the ANC had disappeared.

In 1959 the National Party established universities exclusively for black students, in line with its goal of racial segregation in all educational systems. Students of colour "marched out" of the National Union of South African Students, which was multiracial but still "dominated" by white students. Its origins were also deeply rooted in Christianity: in 1966 the Anglican Church under Archbishop Robert Selby Taylor convened a meeting that led to the University Christian Movement, which became the vehicle for Black Consciousness.

The term stems from W. E. B. Du Bois's evaluation of the double consciousness of black Americans. Du Bois echoed Martin Delany's insistence that black people take pride in their blackness, a line of thought also reflected in Marcus Garvey, Alain Locke and the salons of Paulette and Jane Nardal in Paris. Biko's understanding of these thinkers was shaped through postcolonial writers such as Frantz Fanon, Léopold Senghor and Aimé Césaire.
sections.aims:
Part of the movement's insight was that black liberation would come not only from fighting for structural political changes, as older movements such as the ANC had done, but also from a psychological transformation in the minds of black people themselves. Biko saw the struggle as having two stages, "Psychological liberation" and "Physical liberation". The movement called for resistance to apartheid, freedom of speech and more rights for oppressed black South Africans, but also for black pride and a readiness to make blackness, rather than simple liberal democracy, the rallying point of unapologetically black organisations. It defined black to include other "people of color", most notably the large number of South Africans of Indian descent, and sought "not black visibility but real black participation".

It attacked what it saw as traditional white values, especially the "condescending" values of white liberals, refused to engage white liberal opinion on the pros and cons of black consciousness, and emphasised the rejection of a white monopoly on truth. It asked whites to understand and support, but not to lead, and so rejected the "non-racialism" of the ANC. The ANC viewed white participation as part of enacting the non-racial future it was fighting for; the Black Consciousness view was that even well-intentioned white people often re-enacted the paternalism of their society, and that black people had to gain psychological, physical and political power before non-racial organisations could truly be non-racial. "Black man, you are on your own" became its rallying cry.
sections.events:
The movement formed Formation Schools to provide leadership seminars and placed great importance on decentralisation and autonomy, with no person serving as president for more than one year, although Biko was clearly its primary leader. In 1970 Bennie Khoapa, Barney Pityana, Mapetla Mohapi and Mamphela Ramphele joined Biko in establishing the Black Community Programmes (BCP) as self-help groups, forming out of the South African Council of Churches and the Christian Institute. Through them the movement was involved in staging the large-scale protests and workers' strikes that gripped the nation in 1972 and 1973, especially in Durban.

In 1973 the government began to clamp down, claiming that the ideas of black development were treasonous, and virtually the entire leadership of SASO and the BCP was banned. In late August and September 1974, after rallies in support of the FRELIMO government in Mozambique, many leaders were arrested under the Terrorism Act and the Riotous Assemblies Act, 1956, which allowed the suspension of habeas corpus. Many were not formally charged until the next year, resulting in the "Pretoria Twelve" and the conviction of the "SASO nine". These trials gave members a forum to explain their philosophy and describe the abuses inflicted on them, and far from crushing the movement they led to wider support among black and white South Africans.

The movement heavily supported the protests that led to the Soweto uprising of 16 June 1976, which began when black students were required to learn Afrikaans and many secondary classes were to be taught in it. The protest began as a non-violent demonstration before police responded violently and it turned into a riot. The official number of protesters killed is 176, though estimates range up to nearly 600.
sections.people:
The movement was led by Steve Biko, Mamphela Ramphele and Barney Pityana. Biko, a medical student when it began, was its founder and primary leader, and he became a symbol of the struggle. Bennie Khoapa, Pityana, Mapetla Mohapi and Ramphele joined him in establishing the Black Community Programmes, whose approach to development was strongly influenced by Paulo Freire. Mohapi was a leader of the South African Students' Organisation (SASO) and director of the Zimele Trust Fund, which Biko established officially in 1975. Aubrey Mokoape and Patrick Lekota were among the "SASO nine" convicted in the trials that followed the arrests of 1974. Others named among its important figures include Strini Moodley, Malusi Mpumlwana, the artist Thamsanga Mnyele, the cleric Rubin Phillip, the playwright Mthuli ka Shezi and Barney Simon, founder of The Market Theatre.

The funds for many projects came from fundraising by Father Aelred Stubbs through churches in Europe. The white newspaper editor Donald Woods befriended Biko, left South Africa and exposed the truth behind Biko's death at the hands of police in his book Biko. In the months after the death a new generation of activists, inspired by the Soweto riots and by Biko's death, met alongside members of the movement, among them Bishop Desmond Tutu.

Writers gave the movement its voice. Mongane Serote, Mafika Gwala and Sipho Sempala led in poetry, and Ingoapele Madingoane became its best-known poet-performance artist. Njabulo Ndebele, Miriam Tlali, Mothobi Mutloatse and Mbulelo Mzamane wrote prose, and Adam Small wrote in Afrikaans and English.
sections.outcomes:
The movement's gains were widespread across South Africa. Many black people felt a new sense of pride as it exposed and critiqued the inferiority complex felt by many at the time. Its Black Community Programmes organised community medical clinics, aided entrepreneurs and held "consciousness" classes and adult literacy classes. The Zimele Trust Fund helped newly released political prisoners and their families, gave bursaries and scholarships to activists' children and supported projects such as the Zanempilo Community Health Care Centre.

Assessments of the movement note that it failed to achieve several key objectives. It did not bring down the apartheid regime, and its appeal to other non-white groups as "people of color" gained little traction. Nelson Mandela and his successors downplayed its focus on blackness and emphasised the multi-racial balance needed for the post-apartheid nation. Its community programmes were very small in scope, and its leadership and structure were essentially liquidated by security action.

Critics argued that the movement would stagnate into black racialism, aggravate racial tensions and attract repression, or even perpetuate a racial divide, "apartheid for the Blacks". Others thought it rested heavily on student idealism, with little grassroots support among the masses and few links to the mass trade-union movement. According to Pallo Jordan, "The great tragedy of the Black Consciousness Movement (BCM) was that it was never able to gather and retain much support beyond a narrow band of African intellectuals." In the 1980s rivalry between adherents belonging to Azapo and the United Democratic Front led to deadly violence in black townships, most pronounced in Soweto.
sections.legacy:
On 19 October 1977 the government declared 19 groups associated with the movement illegal, and many members then joined more tightly structured parties such as the ANC, which used underground cells to keep its organisation intact. Meetings to discuss resistance nonetheless continued, and the Azanian People's Organisation (AZAPO), formed in 1978, persists to this day. Other groups sharing its principles followed, including the Congress of South African Students, the Azanian Student Organisation and the Port Elizabeth Black Civic Organisation. In 1980 Pityana formed the Black Consciousness Movement of Azania, an avowedly Marxist group that used AZAPO as its political voice.

The most lasting legacy is described as that of an intellectual movement. AZAPO has been unable to win significant electoral support in modern-day South Africa, but the diffusion of Black Consciousness language and strategy into most corners of black South African politics is seen as a measure of the ideas' strength. They helped organise action beyond any specific organisation, so that when one group's leader was imprisoned, more black South Africans still agreed on the importance of black leadership and active resistance. One assessment holds that Biko and the movement helped give the resistance a culture of fearlessness, and that this spirit fuelled the later street confrontations with police and army.

Even after the end of apartheid, Black Consciousness politics live on in community development projects and "acts of dissent" staged both to bring about change and to develop a distinct black identity.

summary: The Black Consciousness Movement was a South African anti-apartheid movement, led by Steve Biko from the mid-1960s, that sought the psychological liberation of black people through pride and black leadership. Its organisations were banned in 1977, but its ideas spread widely and AZAPO persists.
notes: Start: the article says the movement emerged in the mid-1960s and began to develop in the late 1960s; the University Christian Movement dates from 1966. I used 1966 with circa true. End is null because the article says AZAPO persists and that Black Consciousness politics live on, though it also says the movement is no longer represented by a single organisation.

The lede's sentence about the Soweto uprising is garbled ("both outrage and unrest spread by lesepa voetsek implemented a system of comprehensive local committees"); I left that sentence out. I kept the lede's separate statement that 123 key members were banned by 19 June 1976.

The lede says all BCM-related organisations were banned in 1977 under the Internal Security Amendment Act; the history says 19 groups were declared illegal on 19 October 1977. I used the 19 groups and left out the Act.
Soweto death toll: official 176, estimates up to nearly 600; both given. The lede says 176 child protesters were shot; the history gives 176 as the official number.

The article says Biko was a non-violent activist even though the movement later took up violent resistance, but also that his non-violence may be seen as tactic. I kept only the tactic reading, attributed with 'may be seen'.
The article says the BCM was led by Biko, Ramphele and Pityana, and elsewhere that no person served as president more than a year; kept both.
Left out: the Literature section's poem excerpts (empty in the text), the Lassana Kanté study, the Black Review and Black Viewpoint details beyond the profile, and the Bans section.

The 'a culture of fearlessness' and 'teenagers throwing stones' reading is the article's own assessment, framed as 'one assessment holds'; the stone-throwing line was left out. The 'intellectual movement' and 'strength of ideas' wording is likewise the article's judgement.
